questions.prompt: The storefront's testing guide separates three outcomes: a validation rejection, a transaction failure, and an uncertain completion. Define each, give the example the guide uses and what its test asserts, explain how the browser suite produces an uncertain completion, and say why returning a 503 before the request reaches the API is the wrong way to simulate it.

keyPoints.text: A validation rejection happens before any domain writes.
keyPoints.quote: A validation rejection happens before domain writes.

keyPoints.text: Example: a checkout body with a client-supplied total or duplicate product ID returns 400 and creates no order.
keyPoints.quote: a checkout body with a client-supplied total or duplicate product ID must return 400 and create no order.

keyPoints.text: A transaction failure happens after work may have begun but before commit.
keyPoints.quote: A transaction failure happens after some work may have begun but before commit.

keyPoints.text: The audit-failure tests reject an audit insert and assert that order, item, inventory and receipt changes all roll back.
keyPoints.quote: assert that order, item, inventory, and receipt changes all roll back.

keyPoints.text: An uncertain completion is a committed transaction whose response the browser loses.
keyPoints.quote: the transaction commits, but the browser loses the response.

keyPoints.text: The browser suite intercepts checkout, lets the real server complete it, then aborts delivery, and checks that the frozen attempt remains.
keyPoints.quote: intercepts checkout, lets the real server complete it, then aborts delivery to the page.

keyPoints.text: A 503 before the API tests rejection handling, not recovery of an already committed order; create the failure at the boundary tied to the claim.
keyPoints.quote: That tests rejection handling, not recovery of an already committed order.

questions.prompt: How should you read the storefront's backend test evidence? Explain where the six logged 500s come from and how many requests each test makes, what each of those tests asserts, why a seventh 500 matters and what alternative contract the guide offers, what concurrency tests must assert beyond status codes, and which money cases are tested and why.

keyPoints.text: The auditFailure helper installs a trigger that makes every AuditEvent insert raise.
keyPoints.quote: installs a trigger that makes every `AuditEvent` insert raise.

keyPoints.text: Four tests use it: registration, product create/update/delete (three requests), checkout and cancellation, so six requests fail.
keyPoints.quote: Four tests use it: registration (line 132, one request), product create/update/delete (line 306, three requests)

keyPoints.text: Each asserts a 500 and that nothing persisted.
keyPoints.quote: Each asserts a 500 *and* that nothing persisted.

keyPoints.text: errors.ts logs every 5xx, so a passing run prints exactly six; a seventh means something else failed.
keyPoints.quote: a passing run prints exactly six such lines; a seventh means something else failed.

keyPoints.text: The injected failure could instead map to a controlled 503; only the expected status would change, not the rollback assertions.
keyPoints.quote: the rollback assertions stay the same and only the expected status changes.

keyPoints.text: Concurrency tests must assert exact winning/losing statuses and inspect persisted stock, versions and audits; two non-500 responses are not enough.
keyPoints.quote: A pair of non-500 responses is not enough evidence.

keyPoints.text: Money tests cover 0.10 plus 0.20, excess fractional precision, and an aggregate order exceeding its storage bound.
keyPoints.quote: Money tests include 0.10 plus 0.20, excess fractional precision, and an aggregate order exceeding its storage bound.

keyPoints.text: Valid individual prices do not guarantee a valid total.
keyPoints.quote: Valid individual prices do not guarantee a valid total.

questions.prompt: Debugging from retained evidence in the storefront: what should you record for a failed checkout and what must you leave out, how do you investigate a stale product edit and why must the version not be refreshed automatically, and what does each kind of evidence (component tests, browser tests, production build, database tests) actually prove?

keyPoints.text: Record the request ID, checkout key, customer identity, submitted product IDs and quantities, status and observed order ID.
keyPoints.quote: record the request ID, checkout key, customer identity, submitted product IDs/quantities, status, and observed order ID.

keyPoints.text: Exclude bearer tokens and passwords.
keyPoints.quote: Exclude bearer tokens and passwords.

keyPoints.text: For a stale edit, compare the captured product version with the current version.
keyPoints.quote: compare the captured product version with the current version.

keyPoints.text: Loading current values should be an explicit choice made after exporting the pending draft.
keyPoints.quote: Loading current values should be an explicit choice after exporting the pending draft.

keyPoints.text: Automatically updating the version would conceal a lost-update risk.
keyPoints.quote: Automatically updating the version would conceal a lost-update risk.

keyPoints.text: Component tests verify HTTP failure handling and catalogue role controls; browser tests prove real draft retention and accepted-save feedback.
keyPoints.quote: browser tests prove real draft retention and accepted-save feedback.

keyPoints.text: A production build proves bundling and type compatibility, while a database test proves a different part of the contract; keep them distinct in review.
keyPoints.quote: A production build proves bundling and type compatibility, while a database test proves a different part of the contract.
